content_preview.title: PyPI, Packagist and GitHub Lock Different Parts of a Published Release, GitHub's Only Where Enabled: A Comparison With Four 2026 Incidents
content_preview.summary: The Herald compares PyPI's 14-day limit on new files, Packagist's locked stable-version references and GitHub's opt-in immutable releases with four 2026 incidents it selected; in its reading, the rules cover different ground.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Background

Four supply-chain incidents reported between March and October 2026 involved release tags, release files or newly uploaded versions: two moved git tags, one swapped files on existing GitHub releases, and one uploaded new versions to PyPI with stolen credentials. The four are the Herald's own selection of cases that bear on how a published release can change; they are not a count of all such incidents. Three of the platforms involved, PyPI, Packagist and GitHub, now have rules limi...

recommendations: Publish with the filed clarification record.
Add the Packagist takedown route (maintainer soft-delete, administrator takedown for malware) when describing the rule.
Link the 2026-10/21 release-controls Analysis, which shares the OVHcloud case and GitHub immutable releases.

editor_notes.content_quality: Well structured Analysis (Background, Current situation, Implications) of about 1,874 words with the Herald's reading clearly separated from sourced facts and labelled as such. The thesis (the three rules lock different objects, and none, as documented, addresses a new version published with stolen credentials) is stated as the Herald's own reading and the four incidents are declared the Herald's own selection.
editor_notes.source_verification: Read all 15 snapshots (source-0 to source-14); every sha256 matches the manifest and every status is 200. Quotes: all 24 quoted spans in the body were matched by script against the snapshot text; the one apparent miss (the PyPI code comment) is verbatim once the '#' line markers in legacy.py are removed. Dates and figures checked from raw data: PyPI Warehouse PR 19727 merged 2026-07-08T21:43:58Z (merge commit e0ee5f8, GitHub API), 14-day constant and error message in legacy.py, issue 19726 opened 2026-03-24; Packagist PR 1742 opened 2026-05-27, merged 2026-06-05T06:52:12Z, with the 'will deploy it tomorrow morning' comment on 2026-06-04T15:36Z and no mention of any incident in its text or review comments; GitHub immutable-releases changelog (2025-10-28), docs (tag cannot be moved, assets cannot be modified or deleted, title and notes editable, draft-first publishing guidance) and workflow-lockfiles changelog (2026-10-28) all confirm the article's statements. Incidents: HN Trivy (2026-03-20, 75 of 76 vs 76 of 77, duplicate v0.0.10 explanation, McCarthy quote), LWN (LiteLLM 1.82.7/1.82.8, March 24, 'without changing any existing branches'), BC and HN Laravel-Lang (rewritten tags, StepSecurity 22:32-00:00 UTC, Aikido 233 versions across three repositories vs Socket roughly 700 vs HN more than 700, Socket 'newly published tags'), HN OVHcloud (v0.11.0 to v0.15.0, 12:47 to 14:21 UTC, OpenSourceMalware timeline, customer's pinned SHA-256 CI job, v0.16.0 immutable, setting available since October 2025). Absence claims checked against every snapshot: no cited outlet mentions the Packagist rule; no source reports a case where any of the three rules blocked a change; no source gives an adoption figure for immutable releases. Route note: the BleepingComputer snapshot is an Archive.org fallback capture (sha256 54d7047f3a64...); the live page now returns a Cloudflare 403 and my own Archive.org retries returned HTTP 429, so I could not re-fetch it independently; its claims were read from the stored, hash-verified capture and the central 'rewrote tags' statement is independently carried by The Hacker News. Injection scan: one match (source 9), a false positive documented in the findings. Independence per outlet: The Hacker News (four articles count once), LWN (two articles count once) and BleepingComputer, 3 independent outlets; the PyPI, Packagist and GitHub pages, the code and the PRs are subject pages and not counted. Per case: Trivy 2 outlets, LiteLLM 1, Laravel-Lang 2, OVHcloud 1, PyPI rule 2 items that both restate PyPI's announcement, Packagist rule 0, GitHub feature 0 independent outlets beyond HN's OVHcloud description; the article states each of these. Anthropic disclosure: not required - neither the article nor any passage it cites mentions Anthropic or Claude (hits in snapshots are sidebar headlines and an unused malware path string).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No wrong statement found in the headline, summary or lead. Subordinate omission: the Packagist template that the article cites also describes a takedown route (maintainers can soft-delete a version they own; administrator takedowns for malware, abuse or legal reasons cannot be recovered by maintainers), and BleepingComputer reports Packagist removing the malicious Laravel-Lang versions; the article describes only the immutability and the advice to tag a new version. Filed as a clarification. Also noted: the re-tag badge text refers to 'Packagist's stored snapshot', which does not say whether archive contents are locked, so the article's open question stands.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and attributive throughout; no sensational language; the vendors' and researchers' statements are attributed.
editor_notes.originality: New angle. The Herald's 2026-10/21 Analysis on release controls (GhostAction, OVHcloud, npm trusted publishing) shares the OVHcloud case and GitHub immutable releases, but this article compares PyPI's 14-day rule and Packagist's reference lock with different incidents (Trivy, LiteLLM, Laravel-Lang). The earlier Analysis is not linked in the article; added as a related article in article-meta. The three linked incident articles exist; only the Laravel-Lang one has a corrections record (a Snyk quote and a GBHackers version range) and neither is repeated.
concerns: The Packagist rule and the PyPI rule rest on project pages plus items that restate PyPI's announcement; no independent outlet covers the Packagist rule, as the article says.

The Trivy sentence 'moving tags avoided the notifications a branch change would have triggered' compresses LWN, which attributes the avoided notifications to adding the malware commits without changing any existing branch and says the tags were then force-pushed; I read it as fair but it is a compression.
Headline 'Lock Different Parts of a Published Release' is figurative for PyPI, whose rule blocks new files after 14 days rather than locking existing ones; the body states the rule exactly.
recommendations: Mention the Packagist takedown route when describing the rule.
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Accurate, well-sourced Analysis that meets the Analysis requirements (about 1,874 words, 15 sources, 3 independent outlets counted per outlet, a labelled thesis beyond a tabulation) and is open about which cases rest on one outlet or on project pages alone. Approved with one clarification. Featured candidacy: 2 - cross-ecosystem comparison of how three package platforms lock releases, relevant to a broad audience of maintainers and security teams, though built on project pages and thin per-case outlet coverage
